title: Constitution: Constitution as a Living Document

learn.hook: The Soviet Union had four constitutions in its 74 years. India has had one since 1950 — amended many times, but never replaced. What's the secret?
points: A constitution must be stable enough to protect core values, yet flexible enough to adapt to new circumstances and challenges.
The Indian Constitution has worked for over seven decades: it has been amended more than 100 times but its basic framework remains.

Many countries replaced their constitutions frequently; for example, the Soviet Union adopted new constitutions in 1918, 1924, 1936 and 1977. France has had many constitutions; its present one dates from 1958.
India's Constitution has survived because it balances rigidity and flexibility and because institutions and leaders have respected it.
A 'living document' is one that responds to changing situations while keeping its core identity, like a living organism that grows but stays itself.

example.q: Compare: Country X replaces its constitution every 15 years. Country Y keeps one constitution but amends it when needed. Which approach is more like India's, and why?
steps: India has kept one constitution since 1950.
It has been amended over 100 times to adapt to change.
So India follows Country Y's approach: continuity with change.

learn.reallife: Like a smartphone getting software updates instead of being thrown away every year, the Constitution gets amendments while the core system stays.

learn.hook: To amend the Constitution, Parliament needs not just a majority but a 'double' majority — and sometimes the approval of half the States too.
points: Article 368 lays down the procedure for amending the Constitution. An amendment bill can be introduced only in Parliament (either House); there is no referendum and no special body like a constitutional convention.

Some provisions can be changed by a simple majority of Parliament, like ordinary laws (e.g. creating new States or altering boundaries under Articles 2–4); these are not counted as amendments under Article 368.
Special majority: in each House, the bill must be supported by a majority of the total membership of the House AND two-thirds of the members present and voting.

For federal provisions (e.g. election of the President, powers of Centre and States, representation of States in Parliament, the judiciary), a special majority plus ratification by at least half of the State legislatures is required.
Both Houses must pass the bill separately (no joint sitting for amendments), and the President must give assent. This mix of methods balances rigidity and flexibility.

example.q: The Lok Sabha has 543 members. 480 are present and voting on an amendment bill. How many 'yes' votes are needed?
steps: Condition 1 (total membership): more than half of 543 → at least 272.
Condition 2 (present and voting): two-thirds of 480 = 320.
Both must be satisfied, so at least 320 votes are needed.

learn.reallife: When the GST amendment (101st, 2016) needed both Houses' special majority and ratification by half the States, State assemblies across India voted on it — federal amendment in action.

learn.hook: One amendment raised High Court judges' retirement age from 60 to 62. Another gave you the vote at 18. Not every amendment is earth-shaking — many are practical fixes.
points: Technical or administrative amendments clarify or update provisions, e.g. the 15th Amendment (1963) raised the retirement age of High Court judges from 60 to 62; the 54th Amendment (1986) revised judges' salaries.

Differing interpretations: some amendments were passed because the government and the judiciary read the Constitution differently, e.g. on property rights and the power to amend Fundamental Rights in the 1950s–70s.

Political consensus: many amendments were passed with broad support across parties, e.g. the 52nd (anti-defection, 1985), the 61st (voting age 18, 1988), and the 73rd and 74th (local government, 1992).
So a large number of amendments does not mean the Constitution is weak; often it reflects adaptation and agreement.
Only a few amendments have been deeply controversial.

example.q: Classify: (a) raising HC judges' retirement age; (b) amendments after the courts struck down land reform laws; (c) the 73rd Amendment.
steps: (a) A practical change in service rules → technical/administrative.
(b) Responding to the court's reading → differing interpretations.
(c) Passed with wide support across parties → political consensus.

learn.reallife: When you vote at 18, you are using a right created by the 61st Amendment — passed with support across party lines.

learn.hook: During the Emergency (1975–77), a single amendment changed so much of the Constitution that people called it a 'mini-Constitution'.
points: The 38th, 39th and 42nd Amendments were passed during the internal Emergency (1975–77), when many opposition leaders were in jail. They were widely seen as attempts to override the judiciary and strengthen the executive.

The 42nd Amendment (1976) made wide-ranging changes: it added the words 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' to the Preamble, added Fundamental Duties, extended the term of the Lok Sabha from five to six years, and tried to curb judicial review.
The 39th Amendment sought to place the election of the Prime Minister beyond the scrutiny of courts.

After the Emergency, the 44th Amendment (1978) reversed many of these changes, e.g. restoring the five-year term of the Lok Sabha and adding safeguards to emergency provisions. It also removed the right to property from Fundamental Rights.
These episodes showed both the risk of misusing the amending power and the ability of the system to correct itself.

example.q: List two changes made by the 42nd Amendment and one change made by the 44th Amendment.
steps: 42nd: added 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' to the Preamble.
42nd: extended the Lok Sabha's term from 5 to 6 years (also added Fundamental Duties).
44th: restored the Lok Sabha's term to 5 years (and removed property as a Fundamental Right).
example.answer: 42nd: Preamble words, 6-year Lok Sabha term; 44th: restored 5-year term.

learn.hook: In 1973, the largest bench ever in the Supreme Court — 13 judges — split 7 to 6. The majority view created the 'basic structure' doctrine, which still guards the Constitution.
points: Golaknath case (1967): the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights.
Kesavananda Bharati case (1973): the Court held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot alter or destroy its 'basic structure'.

The Court did not give a complete list; elements identified in various judgments include supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic government, secularism, federalism, separation of powers and judicial review.
The basic structure doctrine is a judicial contribution: it balances Parliament's power to change the Constitution with protection of its core.
It has since been applied to test many amendments, and is now widely accepted as part of India's constitutional practice.

example.q: Parliament passes an amendment making India a State with an official religion. How would the basic structure doctrine apply?
steps: Secularism has been recognised as part of the basic structure.
Under Kesavananda Bharati, Parliament cannot destroy the basic structure.
So the Court could strike down such an amendment.
example.answer: The amendment would be open to being struck down as violating the basic structure (secularism).

learn.reallife: Every time a big amendment is challenged in the Supreme Court, lawyers argue whether it violates the basic structure — a doctrine born in 1973.

teach.praise: Hoot! Parliament can amend, but not destroy the basic structure, thanks to Kesavananda Bharati!
teach.nudge: Which case said Parliament cannot alter the basic structure?

revise.summary: Golaknath (1967) barred amending Fundamental Rights; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) allowed amending any part but not the basic structure, a court-made doctrine whose elements are identified case by case.
focus: Why it is a judicial contribution
remember: Elements: supremacy of Constitution, democracy, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, judicial review
traps: There is no complete written list of basic structure elements
Golaknath did not create the basic structure doctrine

topics.title: The Constitution grows: courts and political maturity

learn.hook: The words 'right to life' in Article 21 are just a few, yet courts have read into them the right to shelter, livelihood, education and privacy. The Constitution grows through interpretation too.
points: The judiciary has expanded the meaning of many provisions, e.g. Article 21's 'life and personal liberty' now includes livelihood, shelter and dignity.
Courts have also set limits, e.g. the Supreme Court held (Indra Sawhney, 1992) that reservations should generally not exceed 50% of seats.
Political maturity: governments and parties have generally accepted judicial verdicts, even unwelcome ones, and the judiciary has respected Parliament's role.
The Constitution thus evolves through three routes: formal amendments, judicial interpretation, and political practice and conventions.
Exercise idea: classify a change as an amendment, a judicial interpretation or a political practice, and explain the basic structure doctrine with the cases.

example.q: Classify: (a) the 73rd Amendment; (b) the Supreme Court reading livelihood into Article 21; (c) the government accepting a judgment it disagreed with.
steps: (a) Change in the text → formal amendment.
(b) New meaning without changing text → judicial interpretation.
(c) Respect for institutions → political maturity/practice.

learn.reallife: When the Supreme Court recognised the right to privacy in 2017, the text of Article 21 didn't change — its meaning grew.

games.title: How did it change?

games.title: Growth check
items: The meaning of Article 21 has been expanded by the courts.
It now includes livelihood, shelter and dignity.
The 50% ceiling on reservations was laid down in the Indra Sawhney case.
The Constitution changes only through formal amendments.
Interpretation and practice also shape it.
Political leaders accepting court verdicts shows maturity of democracy.
It strengthens constitutional government.
Judicial interpretation changes the text of the Constitution.
It changes meaning, not the text.

quiz.q: In which case did the Supreme Court lay down a general 50% ceiling on reservations?
quiz.explain: Indra Sawhney set the 50% limit.
steps: Asked: case setting a general 50% ceiling on reservations.
Lesson: Indra Sawhney (1992).
Answer: Indra Sawhney (1992)

quiz.q: How has the judiciary contributed to the Constitution as a living document?
options: By interpreting provisions like Article 21 to include new rights
quiz.explain: Interpretation expands meaning without changing text.
steps: Asked: how the judiciary keeps the Constitution living.
Lesson: it expands meanings, e.g. Article 21 now includes livelihood, shelter, dignity.
Courts do not pass amendments or conduct elections.
Answer: By interpreting provisions like Article 21 to include new rights

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of 'political maturity'?
options: Governments accepting court verdicts even when they disagree
quiz.explain: Respecting institutions is a sign of maturity.
steps: Asked: an example of political maturity.
Lesson: governments and parties accepted judicial verdicts, even unwelcome ones.
Answer: Governments accepting court verdicts even when they disagree

quiz.q: The Constitution evolves through
options: formal amendments, judicial interpretation and political practice
quiz.explain: All three routes shape the Constitution.
steps: Asked: the routes by which the Constitution evolves.
Lesson: formal amendments, judicial interpretation, and political practice and conventions.
Answer: formal amendments, judicial interpretation and political practice

quiz.q: Recognising the right to livelihood under Article 21 is an example of
quiz.explain: The text did not change; the meaning grew.
steps: Given: livelihood read into Article 21.
Rule: new meaning without changing the text = judicial interpretation.
Answer: judicial interpretation
quiz.mistake: Thinks every new right needs an amendment

quiz.q: A change that alters the meaning but not the words of the Constitution comes through
quiz.explain: Courts change meaning; amendments change text.
steps: Asked: what changes meaning but not the words.
Rule: amendments change text; courts change meaning through interpretation.
Answer: judicial interpretation

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The Constitution of India is described as a living document. Reason (R): It has grown through amendments, judicial interpretation and political practice.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; these modes of growth are why it is called living.
steps: A: the Constitution is a living document – true.
R: it grew through amendments, interpretation and political practice – true.
These modes of growth are why it is 'living', so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see these as modes of growth

quiz.q: Which is a formal amendment rather than an interpretation?
options: Reading the right to shelter into Article 21
quiz.explain: The 61st Amendment changed the text; the others are judicial.
steps: Asked: which is a formal amendment.
Lesson: lowering the voting age to 18 was the 61st Amendment, a change in the text.
Shelter in Art 21, basic structure and the 50% cap are judicial.
Answer: Lowering the voting age to 18

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Can the Constitution change even without an amendment?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Amendments, interpretation and political maturity all help the Constitution grow!
teach.nudge: How have courts helped the Constitution grow without changing its words?

revise.summary: The Constitution grows through formal amendments, judicial interpretation (like expanding Article 21 or the 50% reservation cap) and political maturity, such as governments accepting unwelcome verdicts.
focus: Classifying changes as amendment, interpretation or practice
remember: Indra Sawhney (1992): reservations generally not above 50%
Article 21 now includes livelihood, shelter and dignity
traps: Interpretation changes meaning, not text; amendment changes text
The basic structure doctrine is judicial, not a formal amendment
